title: An experimental validation of a new shape optimization technique for piezoelectric harvesting cantilever beams

sections.heading: An experimental validation of a new shape optimization technique for piezoelectric harvesting cantilever beams
sections.text:
Khaled Mohamed \*, Hassan Elgamal, Sallam A. Kouritem

Mechanical Engineering Department, Faculty of Engineering, Alexandria University, Alexandria 21544, Egypt

Received 26 August 2020; revised 18 October 2020; accepted 13 November 2020   
Available online 29 November 2020

sections.heading: KEYWORDS
1. Introduction
sections.text:
The researchers have been interested in the field of vibration energy harvesting, due to the great need for harvested energy. The harvested energy can be utilized in structural health observing applications to provide the wireless sensors, actuators, and small electronics instruments with the required power. Our aim in this work is to maximize the harvested power from the surroundings required to power such electronic devices and to save batteries and maintenance costs. In 1995 Williams and Yates [1] discovered the energy harvesting of vibration. They designed a base excitation model that produces electrical power using energy harvesting. Piezoelectricity can be defined as a procedure of combining electrical and mechanical performances of definite materials. Piezoelectric materials can couple the electrical and mechanical performances. Piezoelectric effect occurs when mechanical strain is generated on the surface of a piezoelectric material due to mechanical stress. The piezoelectric material can convert that strain to an electrical charge (voltage). There are many types of piezoelectric materials, but the most popular materials due to their high efficiency are Lead Zirconate Titanate PZT, PZT-5A, and PZT-5H [2].

To estimate the device power generation capability, it is essential to add a resistive load in the energy harvesting circuit during both the analytical and the experimental studies [3]. It is important to study the parameters that affect the natural frequency, the behavior of piezoelectric materials, and the vibration source. So, various engineering fields are interested in designing, simulating, and optimizing the vibration energy harvesting devices to maximize their output power [4]. Determination of the device output voltage as a function of base excitation is defined as the piezoelectric energy harvesting modeling. Many researchers studied the output voltage as a function of the base excitation [3].

Optimization of mechanical parameters to maximize power generation has received great attention [5]. Recently, new methods have been utilized to analyze piezoelectric energy harvesting. Lafarge et al. [6] used the Bond Graph approach to simulate the energy harvesting with piezoelectric cantilever fixed on a vehicle suspension. Ramı´ rez et al. [7] investigated an energy harvester to work in a very low-frequency bandwidth. Moon et al. [8] enlarged the broadband using two masses; the first was a tuned proof mass and the second was a conventional proof mass. Hong et al. [9] studied the effect of the neutral plane on the output power of the piezoelectric harvesters. Staaf et al. [10] utilized asymmetry harvesters for harvester self-tuning. Asymmetry was attained by changing the harvester lengths and proof mass weights. Song et al [11] optimized the PVDF-based cantilever by adjusting the harvester geometry to match a definite natural frequency and applied stress. Kim [12] optimized, analytically, the piezoelectric energy harvester parameters such as the aspect ratio and the tip mass to control the main natural frequency of the harvester. Wickenheiser and Garcia [13] optimized the electrical circuit parameters such as the load impedance and electromechanical coupling effect used in the mechanical electrical conversion. Dietl and Garcia [14] optimized the ratio of the tip mass to the beam mass and the base excitation using an empirical optimization program. Recently, Sun and Seo [15] proposed a novel self-tuning vortex-induced vibration harvester with a slidable bluff body. Zhou et al. [16] investigated and optimized piezoelectric energy harvesters with exploiting a curved-beam structure. Deng et al. [17] devolved a synergetic poly-stable technique. Chen et al. [18] presented a piezoelectric energy harvester with a high density for highway traffic applications. Li et al. [19] developed a broadband bending-torsion L-shaped device. The common disadvantages in the previous optimization schemes are the concentration on either mechanical or electrical parameters only and the rough matching and tuning between the natural frequency and the excitation frequency. Shin et al. [20] demonstrated an ultra-wide bandwidth harvester with the automatic resonance tuning (ART) phenomenon. They employed this ART to adjust the harvester’s natural frequency to tune the ambient vibration without the need for an external source. Khazaee et al. [21] presented a creativity concept using geometry and material lay-up of piezoelectric energy harvesters to enhance the output power and widen the frequency. Homayouni et al. [22] designed and optimized the location of masses and of a piezoelectric patch of energy harvesting. Covaci and Gontean[23] presented a review for the energy harvesting current methods. The major problem, in energy harvester design, is to how maximize the output power within the limitations of cost, dimension, and weight. To generate the maximum power, the harvester should employ the mechanical power to maximize strain in the piezoelectric surface as much as possible. Thus, the piezoelectric layer must be distributed such that the produced average strain is the maximum. In this research good linkage between GA optimization and COMSOL optimization module, including both mechanical and electrical parameters, was obtained. Also, the comprehensive shape (T-shaped with variable width) was optimized for the highest power generation per unit volume.

sections.heading: 2.1. Harvester description and mode shape study
sections.text: The power generation efficiency of piezoelectric energy harvesters depends on adjusting their natural frequency to match the vibration source and selecting the appropriate harvester geometry. COMSOL Multiphysics was utilized to study the effects of the harvester parameters on the natural frequency. An Eigen frequency study was conducted to find and to analyze the natural frequencies and mode shapes of the harvester. The model consisted of three layers; the mid-layer was made from structural steel as the metal baseboard. The top and bottom layers material were (PZT-5H) due to its high dielectric constant and piezoelectric coefficient (see Fig. 1-a). The properties of both the PZT and the structural steel were built- in the COMSOL library (user-defined material). The damping ratio was selected to be 0.08. The first four bending mode shapes of the piezoelectric cantilever beam, with $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { \ m m } }$ length, $1 0 \ \mathrm { m m }$ width, and $2 . 1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ overall thickness, are shown in Fig. 1. The results indicated in Fig. 1 show that the values of the first four free-vibration natural frequencies were $1 0 9 . 2 2 \mathrm { H z } , 6 8 3 . 3 1 \mathrm { H z } , 1 9 1 1 . 9 \mathrm { H z } ,$ and $3 7 4 5 . 5 \mathrm { H z }$ ; respectively. Also, the mode shapes shown in Fig. 1 demonstrate that the first mode is dominant with the highest deflection value compared to other mode shapes. The deflection during the first, second, third, and fourth natural frequencies was $z _ { 1 } = 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m } , z 2 = 8 \mu \mathrm { m } , z 3 = 3 \mu \mathrm { m }$ , and $z 4 = 1 . 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ ; respectively. The percentage of first mode deflection ${ z _ { 1 } } ^ { * } 1 0 0 /$ $( z _ { 1 } + z _ { 2 } + z _ { 3 } + z _ { 4 } ) \rangle$ was $8 1 \%$ . This means that $8 1 \%$ of the vibration and electric energy was during the first natural frequency.

sections.heading: 2.2. Harvester parameters study
sections.text:
Three parameters were chosen for the harvester geometry optimization process: length, thickness, and width. The effects of controlling the three parameters on the relationships between them and the natural frequency are demonstrated by Fig. 2. It is observed that, the increase of beam length reduces the resonance frequency, while the increase of beam width and total thickness increases the resonance frequency. The beam length is the major influencing factor, while beam width has relatively less effect. Although the curves represent the influence of single parameter on natural frequency, the trend remains sensible when multiple parameters changes. To design a piezoelectric cantilever beam with a specified natural frequency, for a definite application, the beam size parameters should be adapted.

sections.heading: 3.1. Harvester optimum shape
sections.text:
The main challenge in the design of the piezoelectric cantilever is how to maximize the output power. Several prototypes and extensive experiments with many design processes are required to design and manufacture the harvester. This design approach has a very high cost. So, the application of non-traditional optimization techniques could be much appreciated. In this part, the T-shaped, rectangular, L-shaped, variable width, and triangular cantilever with piezoelectric material were optimized and simulated. The target of this section is to determine the best geometry which gives the maximum output power per unit volume. To maximize the output power, the genetic algorithm (GA) was utilized to optimize the rectangular harvester. During the GA optimization, the power output was utilized as a single fitness function as follows [27]: $$ \begin{array} { r l } & { \mathrm { c } _ { \mathrm { p } } = \frac { 2 \varepsilon \mathrm { b } \mathrm { L } } { \mathrm { h } _ { \mathrm { p } } } } \\ & { \mathrm { P } = \frac { 1 } { 2 \omega _ { \mathrm { n } } ^ { 2 } } \frac { \mathrm { R c } _ { \mathrm { p } } ^ { 2 } \left( \frac { 2 \mathrm { E } _ { \mathrm { p } } \mathrm { d } _ { 3 1 } \mathrm { h } _ { \mathrm { p } } } { \mathrm { k } _ { 2 } \varepsilon \mathrm { a } } \right) ^ { 2 } \mathrm { A } _ { \mathrm { i n } } ^ { 2 } } { \left( 4 \zeta ^ { 2 } + \mathrm { k } _ { 3 1 } ^ { 4 } \right) \left( \mathrm { R c } _ { \mathrm { p } } \omega _ { \mathrm { n } } \right) ^ { 2 } + 4 \zeta \mathrm { k } _ { 3 1 } ^ { 2 } \left( \mathrm { R c } _ { \mathrm { p } } \omega _ { \mathrm { n } } \right) + 4 \zeta ^ { 2 } } } \end{array} $$ According to Zhang [28], to obtain the optimum power, the natural frequency $( \omega _ { \mathrm { n } } )$ was set equal to the excitation frequency $( \omega )$ in equation (2). The simulation results of the various five shapes of cantilever beam using COMSOL are shown in Fig. 3. The Eigen frequency study was investigated to determine the natural frequency and the deflection of the five shapes. The resonance frequencies, output power, electric voltage, the optimum resistance and the stresses of the various shapes were calculated and tabulated in Table 3. The reported results in Table 3 demonstrate that the T-shaped cantilever structure can produce the highest voltage and power during the lowest natural frequency, compared with other shapes. Also, it is observed that the T-shaped geometry is the best shape for piezoelectric based energy harvesting cantilevers with the same volume (3.4 times higher output power as compared to the power of triangular shape), followed by the rectangular shaped cantilever which is the most widespread due to its simple construction and low stress. Fig. 4 shows the relation between the frequency and the power of the various five shapes. The results in Table 3 and Fig. 4 prove that the low frequency gives more power as mentioned by Roundy et al. [30]. The optimization and simulation processes indicated the importance of the electrical parameter optimization (resistance) in power maximization. While the electrical parameters were neglected, in most of the previous optimization researches, this research indicates that the power of the T-shaped was improved due to the resistance optimization from $1 8 ~ \mathrm { m W }$ at $1 0 0 \ \Omega$ (un optimized), to $2 8 \mathrm { m W }$ at $3 1 6 . 3 ~ \Omega$ . ![](images/2d68a9eff939d7a2f4f91727bd7128c338c7916be6448a24fbaea1871141d0f1.jpg) Fig. 6 The FEM modeling of T-shaped with variable width geometry. ![](images/2cb55db878ae1472bfb28e6b055e794606d8d9bfc2636bbc4c456639b7958085.jpg) Fig.7 The power output response of the optimized harvester frequency. ![](images/3700b46035891219f33cd40295ca48656cde64bb5bc1cb0565a83a1ec8aaf4a8.jpg) Fig. 8 The voltage response of the optimized harvester frequency. ![](images/d08b44bfa6197d122198cdf6b4b10694ab89d9faec6739bcdebb81c102801a3a.jpg) Fig. 9 Dependence of the voltage and power output on the resistance. ![](images/bc2acadb7dafac69ac9114a3d354e1283f586f73cf7148e1ac657cc32332ea17.jpg) Fig. 10 Dependence of the voltage and power output on the acceleration.

sections.heading: 3.2. Geometric optimization of T-shaped variable width harvester
sections.text:
Geometric optimization of the cantilever is very important in maximizing the output power and it is still an open tricky problem in the literature. This optimization was considered by Noh and Yoon in [31], Goldschmidtboeing and Woias in [32], and Roundy et al. [33]. The parameters of the geometry used to define the T-shaped variable-width cantilever are demonstrated in Fig. 5. The parameters considered to describe the beam width at the free and clamped sides are $\mathrm { W } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { W } _ { 4 }$ respectively, and that for the beam length is L. The flange widths of the $\mathrm { T }$ are $\mathrm { w } _ { 1 }$ , ${ \bf W } _ { 3 }$ , and $\mathbf { W } _ { 2 }$ which are the left, middle and right width, respectively. Also, the flange length of the T is $\mathrm { L } _ { 1 }$ . The materials and the damping ratio are selected as previous. In this section, the geometric dimensions for a T-shaped cantilever harvester were investigated to find the optimum harvester parameters. According to the previous results the T cantilever gave the highest power per unit volume compared to the other shapes. Also, the T-shape parameters can be modified to produce any of the other shapes. For example, if $\mathbf { w } _ { 1 } = \mathbf { w } _ { 2 } = \mathbf { L } _ { 1 } = 0$ and $\mathrm { \Delta W } _ { 3 } ~ = ~ \mathrm { \Delta W } _ { 4 }$ , the T-shape becomes the rectangular shape while, if $\mathbf { w } _ { 1 } = \mathbf { w } _ { 2 } = \mathbf { L } _ { 1 } = \mathbf { 0 }$ , the T-shape changes into the variable width shape. Also, when $\mathbf { w } 1 = \mathbf { w } 2 =$ $\mathrm { w } 3 = \mathrm { L } 1 = 0$ , the T-shape reduces to the triangular shape and, if $\mathbf { w } _ { 1 } = \mathbf { 0 }$ the T-shape becomes the L-shape.

sections.heading: 3.2.1. Geometric optimization using COMSOL optimization module
sections.text:
The geometric optimization of the T-shaped variable-width harvester was executed using the COMSOL optimization module (BOBYQA). The eight selected geometric parameters, to be optimized, were $\mathrm { w } _ { 1 }$ , $\mathbf { W } _ { 2 }$ , ${ \bf W } _ { 3 }$ , $\mathrm { w } _ { 4 }$ , $\mathrm { L } _ { 1 }$ , L, $\mathtt { h _ { p } }$ , and hs. The electric energy output of the harvester was the objective function to be maximized. BOBYQA, the optimization solver, was utilized in the optimization module. BOBYQA is an iterative algorithm for minimizing a function, in which each iteration employs a quadratic approximation with many advantages, as mentioned by Powell [34]. The natural frequency was constrained to be less than $1 5 0 \ \mathrm { ~ H z }$ and greater than $5 0 \ \mathrm { ~ H z }$ to match the frequency of ring mode of the passenger part vibration and dive line bending vibration as mentioned by [6]. Also, the stress was constrained to be less than the strength of the material. Lower and upper bounds limits and the results of the optimized T-shaped variable-width harvester parameters are shown in table 4. The piezoelectric material with small thickness was utilized to decrease the frequency and increase the power, while the steel with large thickness was utilized to decrease the stress.

sections.heading: 3.2.3. Simulation process of the optimized harvester
sections.text:
The results of the optimized parameters of Table 4 were used to simulate the T-shaped harvester. The total volume of the optimized harvester was assumed to be $1 0 2 5 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ . The base excitation was 1.2 of the gravitational acceleration (g). sections.heading: 4.1. Experimental verification of low frequency and low piezoelectric volume cantilevers
sections.text:
There were three essential objectives of the experimental study of this section. The first was to calculate the AC voltage of a harvester needed to harvest the energy of vibration within a frequency range from 2 to $5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ . The low frequency is the practical frequency of the vehicle suspension as specified by Zhao et al. [37]. Also, the long harvesters (up to $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { m m } }$ long) were utilized in low-frequency applications by [38] and [39]. The second aim was to verify the results of the finite element analysis results. While the last one was to study the effect of increasing the cantilever length and the free tip mass on the voltage and frequency. To study the effect of increasing tip mass and length, two different tip masses were utilized. The first tip mass was $2 6 . 3 \ \mathrm { g }$ and the second was $4 0 . 7 ~ \mathrm { g }$ as the flange of the Tshaped. Fig. 11 shows the first proposed piezoelectric harvester $_ { ( 2 6 . 3 \mathrm { ~ g ~ } }$ tip mass) utilized to harvest the vehicle suspension vibrations.

The piezoelectric energy harvester details, shown in Fig. 11 (a), will be illustrated in the next section. Also, Fig. 11 shows the quarter vehicle model and the two-degrees of freedom suspension vibration model. The piezoelectric harvester is attached to the vehicle axle.

sections.heading: 4.1.1. Experimental setup
sections.text:
Fig. 12(a) indicates the experimental arrangement utilized for the frequency response measurement. To avoid the effect of the change of the cross-section of the material, we developed a COMSOL model with the same arrangement as the experimental part. The piezoelectric cantilevers were fastened on top of a variable frequency shaker (DATHAN Scientific) with an amplitude of $0 . 3 { \mathrm { m } } / { \mathrm { s } } 2$ . Variable resistance was connected to the circuit to select the most suitable resistance. Finally, the output voltage of the harvester was stored in the oscilloscope (ATTEN, ADS 1022C). Fig. 12-b and $- \mathbb { C }$ show the two different harvester ends with the free end attached masses. The tip mass was utilized to control the natural frequency.

Fig. 12 shows the COMSOL models of both tip mass and T-section beams. The two models have the same dimensions. The cantilever harvester base is steel with dimensions $1 9 0 \times 4 0 \times 0 . 2 \mathrm { m m }$ . Two layers are fixed on the top of the steel cantilever. The first layer is brass with a circular shape of $4 1 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ diameter and 0.4 thickness, and it is used as the base for piezoelectric material. The second layer is from piezoelectric material PZT-5H with a circular shape of $2 3 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ diameter and $0 . 2 3 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ thickness. From the advantages of these models, that the volume of the piezoelectric is less than $3 \%$ of the total volume of the harvester.

sections.heading: 4.1.2. Experimental results
sections.text:
This section introduces the results of the experimental setup. The frequency range, in finite element analysis (COMSOL frequency response study), was from 0 to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . Fig. 13 shows the relation between the voltage and the frequency. It demonstrates that the first mode was the principal mode, with a frequency of $2 . 1 9 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , and it was accompanied by the highest voltage which was approximately $2 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ . The sum of the voltages of the second, third, and fourth modes represents about $1 6 \%$ of the total output voltage. So, further experiments were executed based on the first mode only. To study the effects of the length and the tip mass of the beam, the voltage was plotted in Figs. 14 and 15 as a function of the frequency, with the same resistance load $( \mathrm { R l o a d } \ : = \ : 5 0 0 \ : \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ . The experimental results shown by Fig. 14 and Table 6, reveal that the frequency of the beam with a tip mass and length of $1 9 0 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ was $2 . 1 6 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ while it was $2 . 2 5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ for a beam of $1 8 0 \mathrm { m m }$ length.

sections.heading: 4.1.3. Experimental verification of the analytical results of variable width T-shaped cantilever
sections.text:
The main target of this section is to study the effect of increasing the piezoelectric material volume on the output voltage and natural frequency. Also, the best location of the piezoelectric material is to be determined. The six parameters utilized to define the T-shaped variable-width cantilever are shown in Fig. 19. The harvester base was an optimized steel cantilever with the dimensions shown in Table 6.

A circular piezoelectric element with two layers was fixed at the top of the cantilever. The first layer was brass with $4 1 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ diameter and $0 . 4 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ thickness, which represents the base for the piezoelectric material. The second layer was the piezoelectric material PZT-5H with a $2 3 \mathrm { ~ m m }$ diameter and $0 . 2 3 \mathrm { \ m m }$ thickness. The tip mass attached to the free harvester end was $2 0 ~ \mathrm { g }$ . To study the effect of the piezoelectric material volume, three models were investigated both experimentally and with COMSOL as shown in Fig. 20. The three models were with single, double, and triple piezoelectric elements. All elements were fixed at the top layer at different spaces. The elements, of the two elements and three elements models, were connected serially. Fig. 21 shows the frequency response of the T-shaped variable-width cantilever with one element, two elements, and three elements, respectively. It is obvious from Figs. 21 and 22 that increasing the number of piezoelectric elements increases the frequency, output power, and voltage. Also, the piezoelectric element is more effective when it is located beside the fixed end, where the stress and strain are maximum. So, the best location of the piezoelectric material is through the half-length next to the cantilever fixed end. Table 6 indicates that COMSOL simulation results and the experimental results agree well with an error of less than $1 1 . 7 \%$ . Also, many factors may contribute to this error such as fabrication errors, mismatches in the material properties, imperfections in the placement and tilt of the PZT wafers, human error, ambient temperature, and imperfect adhesion between layers as mentioned by Sadegh [40] who proved that many factors contribute to the error between the simulation results and the experimental measurement.

Mesh accuracy and the approximations of the equations utilized by the COMSOL model may be the sources of error in the simulation.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text: The effect of harvester parameters such as length, width, and thickness of the cantilever beam on maximizing the harvested energy using piezoelectric material was studied. A COMSOL Multi-physics, Eigen frequency study, and analytical analysis using MATLAB were set up to determine the resonance frequencies and to estimate the harvester parameter effects. The T-shaped, rectangular, L-shaped, variable width and triangular-shaped cantilevers were optimized and simulated. A single objective function genetic algorithm (GA) optimization methodology was utilized to maximize the output power of the various five shapes. The highest harvested power resulted from the T- shaped cantilever was 3.4 times the power of the triangular shape. Due to its high power per unit volume, the T-shaped variable-width cantilever was selected to be optimized using the COMSOL BOBYQA optimization algorithm. The output power and voltage were $1 8 3 . 2  { \mathrm { ~ m W } }$ and $9 . 6 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ respectively. The COMSOL results were validated using the experimental setup and the effects of tip mass, cantilever mass and piezoelectric material volume were studied. The damping variation resulted from many factors mentioned before caused a presented error between experimental work and the COM-SOL results. Also, for thin plates as the length increases the mesh accuracy decreases. The results proved that increasing the length of the cantilever, tip mass and piezoelectric volume increases the output power.
